5 Medical Checkups I’d NEVER Get After 70 (#1 Is the One Everyone Gets) — Doctor Explains

After 70, some of the most common medical checkups can do more harm than good, especially when you feel perfectly fine. In this video, we look at 5 routine medical tests seniors are often offered at their yearly physical, at a pharmacy or at a church health screening: the whole-body MRI or CT scan, the carotid artery ultrasound, the PSA test for prostate cancer, the urine test without symptoms, and the routine TSH thyroid test that can lead to a thyroid pill for life.
You’ll learn how one small finding on a test can start a chain of follow-up scans, biopsies, antibiotics and new medications, why false alarms become more common after 70, and what the research says about overdiagnosis and overtreatment in older adults. We also cover thyroid medication and bone fracture risk, antibiotics for bacteria in the urine, and PSA screening and biopsy risks after 70.
At the end, you’ll get The Pause Plan, a simple routine to use before your next checkup, along with the questions to ask your doctor about any screening test, so you can decide which tests still make sense at your age.

How to Survive CHOKING When You're Alone After 60 — Do THIS in the First 20 Seconds!


What should you do if you suddenly start choking and there is no one around to help? In this video, we explain important choking survival techniques for seniors and older adults, including what to do in the first critical seconds, when to call 911, and how to respond if you are completely alone.

You’ll learn about choking symptoms, complete airway obstruction, self-rescue techniques, and practical steps discussed in the video, including leaning forward, forceful coughing, chair-assisted abdominal thrusts, wall back strikes, and the emergency floor technique. How to Eat Eggs Correctly If You Have Diabetes — To Keep Your Blood Sugar Under Control

Can you eat eggs if you have type 2 diabetes? Yes—but what you eat with your eggs, how you cook them, what you drink, and when you eat them can make a major difference to your blood sugar response.

In this video, Dr. Ares explains how to build a diabetes-friendly egg breakfast using practical, everyday foods. You’ll learn why eggs are a high-quality source of complete protein, leucine, choline, vitamin D, lutein, and zeaxanthin, and how protein at breakfast may help support better blood sugar control, insulin response, satiety, and the “second meal effect.”

The video breaks down 4 important decisions: what you cook your eggs in, what you eat alongside them, what you drink, and when you eat breakfast. You’ll see why butter, refined carbohydrates, breakfast juice, sweetened drinks, and processed breakfast foods can work against your blood sugar goals—and why avocado, spinach, tomatoes, peppers, mushrooms, water, and unsweetened tea are better choices.

A major focus is the dawn phenomenon—the early-morning rise in blood glucose caused by hormones that signal the liver to release stored glucose. The video explains how this can affect fasting blood sugar and why the timing and composition of your first meal may matter for people with type 2 diabetes.

You’ll also get a simple morning diabetes breakfast routine, including two eggs, half an avocado, non-starchy vegetables, water or unsweetened green tea, plus practical mistakes to avoid when eating eggs with diabetes.

The REAL Reason You Wake Up to Pee at Night After 60! (It's Not Your Bladder)

Struggling with nocturia after 60? It is often not your bladder, but systemic issues affecting your sleep quality.

Waking up multiple times a night is a common concern for older adults, yet it is frequently misattributed to bladder capacity alone. This presentation examines the physiological drivers of nocturnal polyuria, specifically how kidney function, sleep apnea, and metabolic health interact to increase urine production overnight. We look at why the body retains sodium and how evening blood sugar spikes can disrupt your rest.

Managing these symptoms often requires addressing underlying fluid dynamics. We discuss the role of leg edema and how simple adjustments, such as leg elevation before bed, can help redistribute fluid and reduce late-night bathroom trips. By understanding these mechanisms, you can better coordinate with your doctor to improve your overall senior health and sleep quality.

He Died In His Sleep From Doing This — Doctors Beg Seniors To Stop (Heart Attack & Stroke Warning)

What you do in the hours before going to bed may have a greater impact on your heart health than you realize. As we get older, certain nighttime habits can affect blood pressure, sleep quality, circulation, and cardiovascular health. Some warning signs should never be ignored, especially in adults over 60.

In this video, we discuss 5 nighttime habits that may increase cardiovascular risks in older adults, including habits related to alcohol consumption, pain medications, stress, sleeping positions, and ignoring possible warning signs of a heart attack or stroke.

You will also learn why nighttime blood pressure changes matter, how the body's cardiovascular system responds during sleep, and what practical steps may help support better heart health after 60.

In this video, you will discover:

1. Using Alcohol to Fall Asleep

Learn how drinking alcohol before bedtime can affect REM sleep, nighttime blood pressure, heart rate, and the body's natural sleep cycle. Understand why alcohol may be particularly concerning for older adults taking cardiovascular medications.

2. Taking Over-the-Counter Pain Relievers Before Bed

Discover the potential cardiovascular risks associated with NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen. Learn why older adults should discuss regular nighttime pain medication use with their healthcare providers.

3. Going to Bed While Your Stress Response Is Still Active

Understand how stress, cortisol, and adrenaline can affect heart rate and blood pressure. Discover why emotional stress, late-night news, and excessive screen time may interfere with relaxation before sleep.

4. Sleeping in the Wrong Position

Explore how sleeping positions may affect breathing, acid reflux, and circulation. Learn about the potential benefits of side sleeping and practical ways to make your sleeping position more comfortable.

5. Ignoring Warning Signs Before Going to Sleep

Recognize important warning signs that may indicate a heart attack or another cardiovascular emergency, including chest pressure, jaw or arm pain, unexplained shortness of breath, cold sweats, and unusual fatigue. Learn why these symptoms require immediate medical attention rather than waiting until morning.

A Protective Evening Routine for Adults Over 60

This video also explains a practical evening routine, including:
Eating a lighter evening meal.
Reducing stressful news and screen exposure before bedtime.
Staying appropriately hydrated.
Taking prescribed medications as directed.
Preparing a comfortable sleeping environment.
Practicing slow breathing and relaxation.
Paying attention to unusual physical symptoms before going to sleep.

Your heart health deserves attention at every age. Understanding your nighttime habits, recognizing potential warning signs, and discussing health concerns with your doctor can help you make more informed decisions about your well-being.

Have you ever experienced any of these nighttime habits? Which one are you planning to change?** Share your thoughts in the comments. Also, tell us your age and where you are watching from.

One Simple Change to How You Walk That Could Save Your Life After 70

Does your walking feel slower, are your steps getting shorter, or do your feet barely clear the ground? This video explores how walking patterns in older adults may affect balance, mobility, and fall risk after 70—and explains one important technique: lifting your feet and focusing on a heel-first step.

Learn five practical walking exercises for seniors: the Precision Step, Standing Hip Hinge Reach, Toe-Off Calf Press, Forward-Path Gaze Walk, and Threshold Step-Through. These movements focus on stride length, foot clearance, hip strength, calf strength, posture, and stepping accuracy to help support safer, more confident walking.

Discover practical fall prevention tips for seniors, balance exercises for older adults, gait training, mobility exercises after 70, and healthy aging strategies—without needing a gym or special equipment.
IN THIS VIDEO, YOU'LL LEARN:

Why changes in walking speed, stride length, and foot clearance deserve attention.

How walking involves coordination between your brain, nerves, muscles, and cardiovascular system.

What the calf muscle pump does and why it matters for circulation.

Why strength, balance, and gait training can be important as you age.

How to approach gentle walking practice more safely.

Which symptoms, including recurring leg pain with walking, warrant medical evaluation.

When to speak with a doctor or physical therapist before starting new exercises.

IMPORTANT FOR ADULTS OVER 70: A shuffling gait or a change in walking ability is not automatically caused by poor circulation or weak muscles. It can have several causes, including medication effects, joint problems, nerve conditions, neurological disorders, and cardiovascular disease. A new or worsening change should be assessed by a qualified healthcare professional.

Do not force a heel-first landing, deliberately lengthen your stride, or attempt balance exercises that make you feel unstable. Choose movements suited to your abilities and follow your clinician's advice.

YOUR INDEPENDENCE MATTERS

Staying active is an important part of healthy aging, but the right approach depends on your health, strength, balance, and medical history. Evidence-based fall-prevention programs often combine individualized balance training, strength exercises, and assessment of personal risk factors.

For decades, blood pressure targets like 120/80 have been treated as a universal standard. However, more recent research suggests that in older adults, especially those over 75, aggressively lowering blood pressure may come with unintended risks.

In this video, Dr. Michael Kent explains why “lower is not always better” for aging arteries. As arteries stiffen with age, excessively low blood pressure may reduce blood flow to the brain and increase the risk of dizziness, falls, and other complications.

We break down the orthostatic hypotension trap—why blood pressure can appear normal while sitting, yet drop to unsafe levels upon standing—and discuss research-backed ranges that may better support stability and long-term health in seniors.

In this video, you’ll learn:

The “120/80” Trap: Why rigid arteries in older adults may require slightly higher pressure to maintain brain circulation

The Sit-to-Stand Issue: How postural blood pressure changes can increase fall risk

Age-Adjusted Ranges: Why blood pressure targets may differ between healthier seniors and more frail older adults

The Brain Connection: How overly aggressive blood pressure control may affect cerebral blood flow

Doctor-Guided Decisions: Why individualized targets should always be discussed with a healthcare professional

Healthy aging after 55 starts with simple daily habits that support senior health, longevity, strength, brain health, mobility, sleep, and independence.

In this video, Dr. Cale Smith shares 6 golden habits for healthy aging to help adults over 55, 60, and 70 stay active, strong, mentally sharp, socially connected, and independent.

You’ll learn practical healthy aging tips, including daily movement, strength training for seniors, anti-inflammatory nutrition, brain health, social connection, and better sleep.

This video explains why exercise for older adults, muscle strength, balance, and fall prevention are essential for maintaining mobility and independence as you age.

Learn about sarcopenia and age-related muscle loss, simple strength exercises for seniors, and how maintaining muscle can support healthy aging.

Discover how the Mediterranean diet, healthy eating, and anti-inflammatory foods can support overall health, cardiovascular health, and longevity.

We also cover brain health after 60, cognitive stimulation, learning new skills, social activity, loneliness, and the importance of meaningful relationships for healthy aging.

Finally, learn why sleep and healthy aging are closely connected and how better sleep habits can support brain health, recovery, and overall well-being.

If you want to know how to age well, stay healthy after 60, maintain muscle, protect brain health, improve balance, sleep better, and live independently, these six habits are a practical place to start...

Consult your doctor or a qualified healthcare professional before making significant changes to your exercise, diet, sleep, or lifestyle, especially if you have existing health conditions or take medications.

5 Common Pills That Secretly Increase Heart Attack & Stroke Risk After 60!

Are some common medications affecting your heart health after 60? In this video, we examine 5 medication categories that may influence blood pressure, heart rhythm, electrolytes, blood sugar, and cardiovascular risk in older adults—including diphenhydramine sleep aids, diuretics, statins, decongestants, and sulfonylurea diabetes medications.

You’ll learn why OTC sleep aids containing diphenhydramine can have anticholinergic and cardiovascular effects, how diuretics can affect potassium and magnesium, what researchers have found about statins and CoQ10, why pseudoephedrine can raise blood pressure and heart rate, and how sulfonylurea-related hypoglycemia can place additional stress on the cardiovascular system.

The video also explains medication safety for seniors, drug interactions, electrolyte monitoring, low blood sugar, high blood pressure, arrhythmias, cardiovascular risk, and medication reconciliation. Most importantly, this is not a recommendation to stop prescribed medication—the final section shows practical questions to discuss with your doctor or pharmacist.

If you are over 60, take multiple prescriptions or over-the-counter medicines, or have heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes, or cardiovascular risk factors, this medication-awareness guide can help you prepare for a more informed medication review.

Medical Disclaimer: This video is for general health education and medication-awareness purposes only. It is not a substitute for individualized medical advice. Do not stop, change, or reduce any prescription or over-the-counter medication without speaking with your doctor or pharmacist. Medication risks vary according to your health conditions, dose, duration of use, and other medicines you take.
